paragraphs.source_en: If humanity survives the next few centuries, it’s probable we’ll expand into space. People, nations, and the international community have options about how to proceed. The choices we make now—about the pace of expansion and the rules underpinning it—will shape that future in ways we can’t yet imagine. The wrong choices wouldn’t merely slow us down, they might create existential risk for humanity.

paragraphs.source_en: We can’t make these choices properly unless people actually know what the truth is about space settlement. All of it. Not just the size of the rocket or the power needs of a settlement or the available minerals in asteroids, but the big, open questions about things like medicine, reproduction, law, ecology, economics, sociology, and warfare. Detailed treatments that are honest about the severe difficulty of these things are almost invariably left out of books and documentaries about space settlement.

paragraphs.source_en: Why is this discourse so often bad? We believe there are two major reasons. First, the general public knows very little about space. Most people can name exactly one astronaut, and with an appropriate mnemonic can say the planets in order. Outside of a few weirdos, most of us don’t know things like what lunar soil is made of, or what the Outer Space Treaty says, or the history of nuclear weapon detonation in space.

paragraphs.source_en: Given the limited public knowledge of space science in general, knowledge of its weird little cousin—space-settlement science—is almost nonexistent. And that’s where we arrive at the second problem. If you are ignorant about space settlement and want to become educated, many of the articles you’ll read, many of the documentaries you’ll watch, and pretty much every single book on the topic have been created by an advocate for space settlement.
